hints: Look at each test as a clue for a different ion, starting with what gas is released when solution Y is warmed with NaOH.
Warming an ammonium salt with NaOH gives off ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, so X must contain the $\text{NH}_4^+$ ion.
A white silver halide precipitate that dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ points to chloride, so combine that anion with the cation you found.
walkthrough:
**Use the NaOH test to find the cation**

Think of this as the classic test for ammonium ions. Warming with NaOH releases ammonia gas.

$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

**Rule out the aluminium options**

This tells us X contains $\text{NH}_4^+$. That immediately rules out aluminium bromide and aluminium chloride. Also, aluminium salts would give a white precipitate of $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ with NaOH, not a gas.

**Use the silver nitrate test to find the anion**

Adding $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$ to Y gives white precipitate Z. Both $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{AgBr}$ are pale, but their solubility in ammonia is different.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{X}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$

**Use solubility in ammonia to confirm chloride**

Z dissolves in $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ to give a colourless solution. This is the textbook behaviour of $\text{AgCl}$, which forms a soluble complex.

$$\text{AgCl}(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

**Put the clues together**

Cation is ammonium, anion is chloride. Gentle sublimation on heating is also famous for ammonium chloride. So X is $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

options.A: Incorrect. Aluminium bromide contains no $\text{NH}_4^+$, so it would not release $\text{NH}_3$ gas with NaOH. Its bromide would also give a cream precipitate of AgBr which is insoluble in dilute $\text{NH}_3(aq)$.
options.B: Incorrect. Although chloride would give white AgCl soluble in ammonia, aluminium chloride contains $\text{Al}^{3+}$ not $\text{NH}_4^+$. With NaOH it would give white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate, not a gas.
options.C: Incorrect. Ammonium bromide would correctly give $\text{NH}_3$ gas with NaOH, but its anion test fails. $\text{AgBr}$ is a cream precipitate and does not dissolve in dilute $\text{NH}_3(aq)$, only in concentrated ammonia.
options.D: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ explains the gas ($\text{NH}_3$) with NaOH, $\text{Cl}^-$ explains the white AgCl precipitate that dissolves in $\text{NH}_3(aq)$, and solid $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is well known to sublime on gentle heating.
